name: Kojic acid dipalmitate

lead: Kojic acid dipalmitate is an ester of kojic acid, a compound made by fungi, used in cosmetics to lighten dark spots. The palmitate form is oil-soluble and used for stability in formulations.

It helps looks by reducing uneven pigmentation such as melasma and dark patches through inhibition of tyrosinase, the enzyme in melanin formation. Most published work covers formulations (ethosomes, nanoemulsions) tested in the lab and on skin models.

paras: It is an ingredient in topical creams, serums and emulsions, often with other brighteners, used on dark patches over weeks.
Regulators treat kojic acid itself with limits: the EU caps it at 1% in face and hand products. Skin irritation is possible; the ester is a different compound from kojic acid.

chain: Less melanin in dark patches and more even tone
angle.text: KAD is used in creams meant to fade dark spots and melasma and even skin tone.

lead: Kojic acid dipalmitate (KAD) is a diester of kojic acid and palmitic acid used in skin-lightening cosmetics.[1][2] Kojic acid is a metabolite made by fungi such as Aspergillus oryzae.[3]

Papers describe KAD as a tyrosinase inhibitor for hyperpigmentation and melasma, and recent formulation studies load it into ethosomes, nanoemulsions with rosehip oil, and nanocapsules.[2][4] A stability study found KAD degraded faster than kojic acid under oxidative stress and recommended antioxidant excipients.[1]

paras: KAD is described as a tyrosinase-inhibiting agent for hyperpigmentation and melasma.[2] Cosmetic formulations pair it with delivery systems to improve skin penetration.[2][4]

For kojic acid itself, Wikipedia reports the EU limits its use to face and hand products at up to 1%, and that animal studies suggested weak carcinogenicity not thought to reach carcinogenic levels at cosmetic concentrations.[3]
No studies found. Published work is mainly in vitro and formulation studies, including a skin-whitening ethosomal gel evaluated in vitro and in vivo.[2][4]
